target: AG1's claim that school dissection mostly uses already-dead byproducts rather than causing environmental harm
objection: Animal dissection demand is not just a reuse of dead byproducts; it is supplied largely by animals caught in the wild, and that live-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG1's implicit assumption that sourcing animals for dissection is ethically acceptable because they are dead byproducts
objection: The methods used to supply dissection animals are inhumane and harm animals, making dissection ethically and environmentally problematic.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is necessary for biology or medical education
objection: Animal dissection is not required to meet major biology standards and is not needed for physician training, since AP Biology, NGSS, and U.S./Canadian medical schools do not require it.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is educationally valuable because alternatives are inferior
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations teach anatomy and biology equally well or better, so students can learn the same material without animal dissection.

target: AG2's claim that dissection primarily relies on live wild-capture and therefore drives biodiversity loss
objection: Most dissection specimens are already-dead byproducts, so school dissection demand is predominantly met without live wild-capture and does not meaningfully drive biodiversity loss the way AG2 claims.

target: AG1's rebuttal that dissection specimens are mostly already-dead byproducts
objection: The claim that most school dissection specimens are dead byproducts is false if dissection supply actually relies substantially on live wild-captured animals.

target: AG2's environmental objection to dissection
objection: Even if dissection is criticized environmentally, the key issue is whether it truly depends on live wild-capture; if it does not, then the biodiversity-loss objection is not decisive against dissection.

target: AG1's claim that dissection is safe and acceptable when classes meet ethical/safety standards
objection: School dissection can create realistic safety risks because preserved tissues and chemical/biohazard waste require controls that classrooms may fail to maintain reliably.

target: AG1's assumption that dissection can be justified under normal classroom conditions
objection: There is evidence that many school lab practices fall short on PPE, ventilation, and waste handling, so some dissections are unsafe or violate required safety standards.

target: AG1's claim that alternatives cannot provide the same learning as dissection
objection: Synthetic models and simulations can replace dissection for the relevant educational goals, so dissection is not necessary as a learning method.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives can replace dissection for all relevant learning
objection: Alternatives do not give students the same hands-on practice with real-specimen lab safety, including handling biological material and proper disposal/decontamination procedures.

target: AG2's broader objection that dissection should be avoided because alternatives exist
objection: In many schools, alternatives are not reliably available or implementable due to budget, technology, or resource limits, so dissection may be the only feasible way to provide hands-on anatomy learning.

target: AG1's claim that dissection merely uses unavoidable byproducts and is therefore ethically benign
objection: Typical dissection supply chains rely on inhumane wild-capture and harm animals, so dissection is not just harmless use of existing byproducts.

target: AG1's claim that safety compliance can make dissection acceptable
objection: Using inhumane sourcing methods violates required ethical standards regardless of classroom handling procedures, so ethical compliance is not satisfied just by supervising the lab.

target: AG2's claim that models and simulations fully replace the educational value of dissection
objection: Models and simulations cannot reproduce the tactile, three-dimensional experience of cutting and tracing real anatomical structures through an actual specimen.

target: AG1's claim that dissection offers unique educational value
objection: If a practice relies on inhumane sourcing and humane alternatives exist, then any educational value does not justify using it under required ethical animal-use standards.

target: AG2's claim that dissection is unnecessary because alternatives teach required content
objection: Dissection provides training in scientific inquiry skills such as observing, measuring, recording, and using real specimen evidence, which typical alternatives do not replicate as fully.

target: AG1's claim that AP/NGSS not requiring dissection weakens the case against it
objection: The fact that major standards do not require dissection supports the conclusion that it is unnecessary and should not be imposed when alternatives teach the content well.

target: AG1's reliance on educational value to justify dissection
objection: Because dissection supplies are commonly obtained through inhumane wild-capture and harm animals and ecosystems, the practice carries substantial welfare and biodiversity costs that outweigh any non-unique educational benefit.

target: AG2's claim that alternatives make dissection unnecessary
objection: Dissection gives students real-specimen, tactile, three-dimensional anatomical understanding that alternatives generally cannot fully duplicate.

target: AG2's claim that sourcing harms make dissection unacceptable
objection: If most specimens are already-dead byproducts, then dissection is mainly repurposing existing dead animals rather than driving the wild-capture harms emphasized by the opposition.

target: AG1's assumption that byproduct sourcing avoids ethical problems
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, the broader dissection supply chain still commonly uses inhumane wild-capture, so the ethical problem remains.

target: AG2's claim that typical school dissection is sourced through harmful wild-capture
objection: Most dissected animals are already-deceased byproducts, so the typical school dissection supply chain is not primarily based on live wild-capture.

target: AG2's claim that dissection should be banned because it lacks unique educational value and has sourcing harms
objection: Dissection does have unique specimen-based learning value, and when the specimens are already-deceased byproducts the sourcing harms are substantially reduced.

target: AG1's claim that byproduct sourcing makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: Using inhumane wild-capture to supply dissection animals violates required ethical standards, and those standards are not satisfied merely because some specimens may be byproducts.

target: AG2's claim that dissection sourcing necessarily causes major biodiversity and welfare harm
objection: When dissection uses already-deceased byproducts, the harms from wild-capture-driven sourcing are greatly reduced rather than inherent to the practice.

target: AG1's claim that dissection can be justified if it is educationally useful and safely conducted
objection: If the typical sourcing of dissection animals is inhumane and harmful, then the practice still violates ethical standards even if the classroom procedure itself is managed safely.

target: AG2's claim that dissection is unnecessary and should therefore be banned
objection: Dissection can provide distinctive hands-on learning benefits, and if its sourcing harms are minimized through use of already-deceased byproducts, the case for a general ban is weakened.

target: AG2's assumption that the weak-negation exception is met in every dissection class
objection: The objection depends on the class actually using live wild-captured animals or violating safety/ethical requirements; if a class uses already-deceased byproducts and follows required standards, the exception does not apply.

target: AG1's claim that schools can avoid the ethical problem by relying on byproducts
objection: If the dissection supply chain typically depends on wild-captured animals, then schools using those specimens are still using animals obtained through inhumane methods.

target: AG2's claim that dissection should be banned because its sourcing is harmful
objection: Dissection is a productive educational practice when it uses already-deceased byproducts and is conducted safely and ethically, so the presence of possible sourcing harms does not automatically justify a ban.

target: AG1's claim that safe, ethical, byproduct-based dissection is acceptable
objection: Because the typical supply chain is inhumane and harmful, school dissection generally violates required ethical standards and cannot be assumed acceptable.

target: AG2's claim that dissection animals are usually obtained through inhumane methods
objection: Dissection requires real specimen handling and can offer unique tactile and 3D learning, so it remains educationally justified when using already-deceased byproducts rather than live-captured animals.

target: AG2's conclusion that students should not dissect animals at all
objection: If dissection is conducted safely, ethically, and with appropriately sourced already-deceased specimens, then students should still dissect animals as part of biology education.
